Period schedule:

Total: 8 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: Why Does the Diagonal Square Double the Area?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 2.1, p.34
textbook_items_in_class.description: Why should the extension of the vertical and horizontal sides of the original square pass through the vertices of the dotted (doubled) square?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity 1 (Doubling a Square Using Paper), p.35
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cut two identical squares of paper; cut Square 1 along diagonals into 4 triangular pieces (labelled 1–4) and Square 2 into 4 pieces (5–8); arrange pieces 5, 6, 7, 8 around intact Square 1 to form a square with double the area.

time_bands.activity: Pose Baudhāyana's opening question: how can one construct a square with exactly double the area of a given square? Students sketch a unit square, double its side, and compare areas — discovering that doubling the side gives four times the area, not twice.

Guide students through the geometric reasoning: draw the diagonal of the unit square and tilt a new square on that diagonal. Using east-west and north-south auxiliary lines, students count that the original square contains two small triangles while the tilted square contains four, establishing the 2:1 area ratio. Address Math Talk, section 2.1, p.34 ("Why should the extension of the vertical and horizontal sides of the original square pass through the vertices of the dotted (doubled) square?") through class discussion.

Students carry out Activity 1 (Doubling a Square Using Paper), p.35 ("Cut two identical squares of paper; cut Square 1 along diagonals into 4 triangular pieces....") in pairs: cut, label, and rearrange the eight triangular pieces to form the doubled square. Groups share observations and articulate in their own words why the area is exactly doubled.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who argue that a larger-looking square must have more than double the area — the triangle-counting argument (two vs. four congruent triangles) is the corrective, and pressing 'how do you know?' keeps the reasoning rigorous. The extension sequence doubling to areas 2, 4, 8 (each being the square on the diagonal of the previous) can be mentioned as a natural follow-up if groups finish early.
materials: Plain paper (two congruent squares per pair)

periods.activity_title: Folding Inward to Find the Half-Area Square

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity 2 (Halving a Square Using Paper), p.36
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cut out a square from paper; fold it inward such that crease lines pass through midpoints of the four sides to obtain quadrilateral PQRS, which is a square with half the area. Verify using diagonal properties and triangle congruence.

time_bands.activity: Open with the reverse of the doubling question: if the diagonal of a square produces a square of double the area, what construction produces a square of half the area? Students predict and sketch, then share predictions with a partner.

Students perform Activity 2 (Halving a Square Using Paper), p.36 ("Cut out a square from paper; fold it inward such that crease lines pass through midpoints of the four sides....") individually, locating midpoints by folding, producing quadrilateral PQRS. They then unfold to examine the crease lines and auxiliary east-west and north-south lines.

Class works through the geometric proof: using diagonal properties and triangle congruence, students justify that PQRS is a square and that its area is exactly half the outer square. Students write a two-sentence explanation of why the congruent corner triangles establish the halving, then compare explanations in pairs.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that the diagonal of a square produces a square of double the area, students are now building the symmetric result. A common error is claiming PQRS looks like a square without verifying all angles are right angles — insist on the angle-complementarity argument using triangle congruence before accepting the conclusion.

textbook_segments.title: Hypotenuse of an Isosceles Right Triangle

periods.activity_title: From Area Doubling to √2: Naming the Hypotenuse

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This, section 2.3, p.39
textbook_items_in_class.description: Can √2 be expressed as a fraction m/n where m and n are counting numbers? Reason using prime factorization of square numbers.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.3, p.39
textbook_items_in_class.description: Two identical square papers are each cut diagonally into two triangles (4 pieces total labelled 1–4). Arrange these pieces to create a square with double the area of either original square.

time_bands.activity: Define hypotenuse as the side opposite the right angle. Apply the doubling result: since the diagonal of a unit square produces a square of area 2, the hypotenuse c of an isosceles right triangle with legs of length 1 satisfies c² = 2. Derive the general formula c² = 2a² for equal-side length a. Walk through Example 1, section 2.3, p.40 ("Find the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle whose equal sides have length 12....") step by step.

Investigate the decimal nature of √2 through successive bounding: establish 1 < √2 < 2, then 1.4 < √2 < 1.5, then 1.41 < √2 < 1.42, and 1.414 < √2 < 1.415 by checking squares of boundary decimals. Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 2.3, p.39 ("Two identical square papers are each cut diagonally into two triangles....") to anchor the area interpretation.

Work through the irrationality of √2: first via a last-digit argument for terminating decimals, then via the prime-factorization proof in Try This, section 2.3, p.39 ("Can √2 be expressed as a fraction m/n where m and n are counting numbers?"). Students record the two distinct proof strategies in their own words and discuss which they find more convincing.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent confusion is treating √2 as approximately 1.41 and then claiming it terminates — the bounding exercise is designed to show √2 escapes every boundary pair, and the prime-factorization argument then gives a watertight proof. Example 2, section 2.3, p.40 (finding equal sides when the hypotenuse is √72) is a useful self-study pointer for students who want a reverse-direction worked example.
materials: Calculator (optional, for checking squares of decimals)

textbook_segments.title: Hypotenuse of an Isosceles Right Triangle

periods.activity_title: Computing and Bounding Hypotenuses in Practice

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.3, p.39
textbook_items_in_class.description: The length of the two equal sides of an isosceles right triangle is given. Find the length of the hypotenuse and find bounds with at least one digit after the decimal point. (i) 3, (ii) 4, (iii) 6, (iv) 8, (v) 9.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.3, p.40
textbook_items_in_class.description: The hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle is 10. Find its other two sidelengths.

time_bands.activity: Brief recap by having students state c² = 2a² aloud and re-derive it from the area-doubling argument. Pose a quick mental check: if equal sides are 5 units, between which two whole numbers does the hypotenuse fall? Collect oral answers to check readiness.

Students work through Figure it Out Q2, section 2.3, p.39 ("The length of the two equal sides of an isosceles right triangle is given. Find the length of the hypotenuse and find bounds....") for all five cases independently, then compare bounds with a partner. Discuss which cases produce 'nicer' decimals and why.

Class tackles Figure it Out Q3, section 2.3, p.40 ("The hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle is 10. Find its other two sidelengths.") using the hint about the square composed of two such right triangles. Students write a complete solution showing the area reasoning step, then a volunteer presents to the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often skip the bounding step and write a decimal approximation directly — insist on the inequality form (e.g., 4.2 < √18 < 4.3) as the expected answer format for Q2, since the irrationality result means no terminating decimal is exact. For Q3, students who forget the hint can be prompted: 'What shape do two congruent isosceles right triangles form when placed hypotenuse-to-hypotenuse?'

periods.activity_title: Baudhāyana's General Proof: Two Squares into One

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity 3 (Combining Two Squares Using Paper), p.45
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cut out and join two different-sized squares (sides a and b); make two cuts to produce three pieces; rearrange the three pieces into a larger square of side c. Then draw a right triangle using the two smaller squares and a square on the hypotenuse, and cover it with the pieces.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.4, p.47
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the constructions seen in the chapter, how would you construct a square whose area is triple the area of a given square? Five times the area of a given square?

time_bands.activity: Introduce Baudhāyana's Śulba-Sūtra Verse 1.12: combining two different squares into one. Students sketch two different-sized squares side by side, label sides a and b, and predict what the side of the combined square might be. Share predictions.

Students perform Activity 3 (Combining Two Squares Using Paper), p.45 ("Cut out and join two different-sized squares (sides a and b); make two cuts to produce three pieces; rearrange the three pieces into a larger square of side c....") in pairs. As they handle the pieces, they identify the right triangle with legs a and b and the square on the hypotenuse, discovering the area identity concretely.

Class constructs the geometric proof: four congruent right-triangle copies are arranged around the tilted square to fill the outer square; all four sides of the inner figure are equal (congruent triangles) and all angles are right angles (complementarity argument). Students reach a² + b² = c² and articulate it as Baudhāyana's Theorem. Pose Figure it Out Q3, section 2.4, p.47 ("How would you construct a square whose area is triple the area of a given square?....") for class discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established c² = 2a² for isosceles right triangles, students now meet the general case — name this connection explicitly so the generalisation feels earned. The most common error is assuming the inner tilted figure is a square without verifying the angle condition; press the complementarity argument (two acute angles of a right triangle sum to 90°) before accepting the conclusion.
materials: Coloured paper (two different-sized squares per pair)

periods.activity_title: Applying a² + b² = c² and Hunting Integer Triples

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.4, p.47
textbook_items_in_class.description: If a right-angled triangle has shorter sides of lengths 5 cm and 12 cm, what is the length of its hypotenuse? First draw and measure, then verify using Baudhāyana's Theorem.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.4, p.47
textbook_items_in_class.description: If a right-angled triangle has a short side of 8 cm and hypotenuse of 17 cm, what is the length of the third side? Draw, measure, then verify using Baudhāyana's Theorem.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.4, p.47
textbook_items_in_class.description: Let a, b, c denote the sides of a right triangle (c = hypotenuse). Find the missing sidelength: (i) a=5, b=7; (ii) a=8, b=12; (iii) a=9, c=15; (iv) a=7, b=12; (v) a=1.5, b=3.5.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 2.5, p.48
textbook_items_in_class.description: List down all the Baudhāyana triples with numbers less than or equal to 20.

time_bands.activity: Apply Baudhāyana's Theorem a² + b² = c² to the worked example Worked example (Using Baudhāyana's Theorem), section 2.4, p.47 ("Make a right-angled triangle with shorter sides 3 cm and 4 cm; apply a² + b² = c²: 9 + 16 = 25, so c = 5 cm...."), then students solve Figure it Out Q1, section 2.4, p.47 ("If a right-angled triangle has shorter sides of lengths 5 cm and 12 cm, what is the length of its hypotenuse?....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 2.4, p.47 ("If a right-angled triangle has a short side of 8 cm and hypotenuse of 17 cm, what is the length of the third side?....") individually, drawing and measuring before computing.

Students work through Figure it Out Q4, section 2.4, p.47 ("Let a, b, c denote the sides of a right triangle (c = hypotenuse). Find the missing sidelength....") for all five cases in pairs, attending carefully to whether the missing quantity is a leg or the hypotenuse. Responses are compared and errors discussed.

Introduce integer-sided right triangles (Baudhāyana triples). Students respond to Math Talk, section 2.5, p.48 ("List down all the Baudhāyana triples with numbers less than or equal to 20.") in small groups, working systematically. Groups share lists and the class consolidates a complete set, noting which are scaled versions of others.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error when finding missing legs (rather than the hypotenuse) is adding instead of subtracting — remind students that c² = a² + b² means the leg is found via subtraction, not addition. The integer-triple listing task at the close naturally raises the question of whether there is a pattern, which the next portion of the chapter will address through the odd-square identity.

periods.activity_title: Generating Triples, Primitive vs. Scaled, and Fermat's Challenge

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.5, p.50
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 5 more Baudhāyana triples using the odd-square method (i.e., find odd perfect squares, identify n, and use (n−1)² + (2n−1) = n²).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.5, p.50
textbook_items_in_class.description: Does the odd-square method yield non-primitive Baudhāyana triples?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.5, p.50
textbook_items_in_class.description: Are there primitive Baudhāyana triples that cannot be obtained through the odd-square method? If yes, give examples.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the odd-square identity (n−1)² + (2n−1) = n² and demonstrate with n=5 giving (3,4,5) and n=13 giving (5,12,13). Students then work on Figure it Out Q1, section 2.5, p.50 ("Find 5 more Baudhāyana triples using the odd-square method....") individually, then share results. Class discusses and proves algebraically that every triple generated this way is a valid Baudhāyana triple.

Explore primitive vs. non-primitive triples using Figure it Out Q2, section 2.5, p.50 ("Does the odd-square method yield non-primitive Baudhāyana triples?....") and Figure it Out Q3, section 2.5, p.50 ("Are there primitive Baudhāyana triples that cannot be obtained through the odd-square method?...."). Groups examine (8,15,17) and (7,24,25) and check whether the odd-square method generates them. Class reaches the conclusion about what the method covers and what it misses.

Transition to section 2.6: present Fermat's Last Theorem — inspired by infinitely many Baudhāyana triples, Fermat conjectured no solution exists for xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ with n > 2. Share Fermat's marginal note story, 300 years of failed proofs, and Wiles's 1994 solution after setting himself the goal as a child. Class discusses: what does an open problem in mathematics reveal about the nature of mathematical knowledge?

periods.teacher_notes: Students often assume the odd-square method generates all primitive triples — Q3 is designed to correct this, so allow groups to genuinely check before revealing examples like (8,15,17). When presenting Fermat's Last Theorem, the historical narrative naturally raises epistemic questions about proof and conjecture that are worth a brief class discussion; keep it focused on the mathematical idea rather than biography alone.

textbook_segments.title: Further Applications of the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem

periods.activity_title: Lotus Stems, Rhombuses, and Grid Squares: The Theorem in Action

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.7, p.52
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the diagonal of a square with sidelength 5 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.7, p.52
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the missing sidelengths in the following right triangles (six diagrams with known values: sides 7 and 9; sides 4 and 10; sides 40 and 41; sides 10 and √200; sides 10 and √150; sides 27 and 45).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.7, p.53
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the sidelength of a rhombus whose diagonals are of length 24 units and 70 units.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 2.7, p.53
textbook_items_in_class.description: (i) Using dots of a grid as vertices, create squares of area (a) 2, (b) 3, (c) 4, (d) 5 sq. units. (ii) Suppose the grid extends indefinitely — what are the possible integer-valued areas of squares you can create?

time_bands.activity: Open with Bhāskarāchārya's Līlāvatī lotus problem: a stem of length x+1 with tip 1 unit above water, touching the water surface 3 units away when bent. Set up the right triangle (legs 3 and x, hypotenuse x+1) and solve: 9 + x² = (x+1)², giving x = 4 units depth. Students verify by substitution. Then solve Figure it Out Q1, section 2.7, p.52 ("Find the diagonal of a square with sidelength 5 cm.").

Students work through Figure it Out Q2, section 2.7, p.52 ("Find the missing sidelengths in the following right triangles (six diagrams with known values: sides 7 and 9; sides 4 and 10; sides 40 and 41; sides 10 and √200; sides 10 and √150; sides 27 and 45).") in pairs, attending to which side is the hypotenuse in each diagram. Then take up Figure it Out Q3, section 2.7, p.53 ("Find the sidelength of a rhombus whose diagonals are of length 24 units and 70 units."), using the property that a rhombus's diagonals bisect each other at right angles to form four right triangles.

Students explore Figure it Out Q8, section 2.7, p.53 ("Using dots of a grid as vertices, create squares of area (a) 2, (b) 3, (c) 4, (d) 5 sq. units....") on dot-grid paper: drawing tilted squares on the grid whose areas are computed via the theorem. The open question — which integer areas are achievable? — is posed as a Math Talk discussion, connecting back to the chapter's geometric theme of squares built on right-triangle sides.

periods.teacher_notes: The rhombus question (Q3) frequently trips students who do not recall that the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other perpendicularly — prompt with a quick diagram if needed, since this is a properties-of-quadrilaterals result the class will have met before. The grid-square exploration in Q8 is open-ended by design; expect a range of areas and celebrate the pattern (sums of two squares) as a beautiful payoff of the chapter's geometric thread.

items.prompt: Fermat's Last Theorem states that xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ has no solution in positive integers when n is greater than 2. Who provided the first complete, accepted proof of this theorem, and in which century did that proof appear?

options.label: A
options.text: Pierre de Fermat, in the 17th century

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Andrew Wiles, in the 20th century (his proof was completed in 1994).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the historical narrative from section 2.6: Fermat conjectured the result in the 17th century; Wiles proved it in 1994.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses the conjecturer (Fermat) with the prover, not distinguishing between posing a problem and solving it.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student conflates Baudhāyana's earlier work on integer-sided right triangles with the much later question about higher powers.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student associates the theorem with Bhāskarāchārya, perhaps because his Līlāvatī appears in the same chapter, but Bhāskarāchārya did not address Fermat's problem.

inclusivity.support: Re-read the section 2.6 narrative and note the three mathematicians mentioned and their centuries.
inclusivity.challenge: In your own words, explain why the existence of infinitely many Baudhāyana triples makes Fermat's conjecture for n > 2 surprising rather than obvious.

exercise.description: List down all the Baudhāyana triples with numbers less than or equal to 20.

items.prompt: A square has its diagonal drawn, and a new square is constructed with that diagonal as its side. Explain, using the triangle-counting argument from the chapter, why the new square has exactly twice the area of the original square.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Drawing horizontal and vertical lines through the tilted square shows that the original square is made up of 2 congruent right triangles, while the new square on the diagonal is made up of 4 such congruent triangles. Since all four triangles are congruent, the new square contains twice as many as the original, so its area is exactly double.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the auxiliary east-west and north-south lines to count that the tilted square contains four congruent triangles while the original contains two.

inclusivity.support: Sketch the original square, draw its diagonal, and use horizontal and vertical lines to divide the figure into triangles before writing your explanation.
inclusivity.challenge: Extend your argument: if you build a square on the diagonal of the doubled square, show that its area is 4 times the original, and describe the general pattern.

exercise.description: Why should the extension of the vertical and horizontal sides of the original square pass through the vertices of the dotted (doubled) square?

items.prompt: Points P, Q, R, S are the midpoints of the four sides of a square. Explain why the quadrilateral PQRS is itself a square and why its area is exactly half the area of the outer square.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each side of PQRS is the hypotenuse of a right triangle formed by two half-sides of the outer square. Since all four outer sides are equal, these right triangles are congruent, so all four sides of PQRS are equal. The four corner triangles outside PQRS are congruent, and each angle of PQRS equals 90° by the complementarity of the two acute angles of these right triangles. Therefore PQRS is a square. The four corner triangles together fill exactly half the outer square (two triangles = one half-side rectangle), so PQRS has half the area.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use congruence of the four corner right triangles to establish equal sides and right angles, then compute areas by noting the four triangles fill exactly half the outer square.

inclusivity.support: Work with a partner: one person names a property of PQRS (equal sides or right angles), the other explains why it follows from the midpoint construction.
inclusivity.challenge: What if P, Q, R, S divide the sides in ratio 1:2 instead of 1:1? Predict whether the inner quadrilateral is still a square and reason about its area.

exercise.book_ref: Activity 2 (Halving a Square Using Paper), p.36
exercise.description: Cut out a square from paper; fold it inward such that crease lines pass through midpoints of the four sides to obtain quadrilateral PQRS, which is a square with half the area. Verify using diagonal properties and triangle congruence.

items.section_title: Hypotenuse of an Isosceles Right Triangle
items.prompt: Prove that √2 cannot be expressed as a fraction m/n where m and n are positive integers. Use the prime-factorisation argument from the chapter in your proof.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Assume √2 = m/n in lowest terms, so 2 = m²/n², giving m² = 2n². In the prime factorisation of any perfect square, every prime appears an even number of times. The left side m² has the prime 2 appearing an even number of times. The right side 2n² has 2 appearing an odd number of times (one more than the even count from n²). This is a contradiction, so no such fraction m/n exists.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the prime-factorisation parity argument: m² = 2n² forces 2 to appear an odd number of times on the right and an even number on the left, a contradiction.

inclusivity.support: Start by writing out what 'prime factorisation of a perfect square' means with a small example (e.g., 36 = 2² × 3²), then apply the same idea to m² and n².
inclusivity.challenge: Adapt your argument to show that √3 is also irrational, identifying which step changes and which stays the same.

exercise.description: Can √2 be expressed as a fraction m/n where m and n are counting numbers? Reason using prime factorization of square numbers.

items.prompt: Four congruent right triangles with legs a and b are arranged around a tilted quadrilateral to fill a large square of side (a + b). Explain, using angle complementarity, why the inner quadrilateral must be a square rather than merely a rhombus.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each interior angle of the inner quadrilateral is formed at a corner where two acute angles of the right triangles meet. Since the two acute angles of any right triangle sum to 90°, their sum at each corner of the inner figure is 90°. Combined with the fact that all four sides are equal (the triangles are congruent), the inner figure has four equal sides and four right angles, which makes it a square, not merely a rhombus.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use angle complementarity (acute angles of a right triangle sum to 90°) to show each interior angle of the inner quadrilateral is a right angle, upgrading 'rhombus' to 'square'.

inclusivity.support: Draw one corner of the large square and label the two acute angles of the right triangle that meet there; then find the angle left over for the inner quadrilateral's corner.
inclusivity.challenge: What if the four triangles were scalene but not right-angled — would the inner quadrilateral still be a square? Reason about which property breaks down first.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.4, p.47
exercise.description: Using the constructions seen in the chapter, how would you construct a square whose area is triple the area of a given square? Five times the area of a given square?

items.prompt: Using the identity (n − 1)² + (2n − 1) = n², explain how to generate a Baudhāyana triple whenever 2n − 1 is a perfect square, and verify with the case n = 13.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The identity (n − 1)² + (2n − 1) = n² shows that (n − 1), the square root of (2n − 1), and n form a Baudhāyana triple when 2n − 1 is a perfect square. For n = 13: 2(13) − 1 = 25 = 5², so the triple is (12, 5, 13). Check: 12² + 5² = 144 + 25 = 169 = 13². ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Substitute n = 13 into (n − 1)² + (2n − 1) = n² and verify that 144 + 25 = 169.

inclusivity.support: First confirm the identity holds for n = 5 (giving the triple 3, 4, 5), then repeat the same substitution steps for n = 13.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the next value of n greater than 13 for which 2n − 1 is a perfect square, state the resulting triple, and determine whether it is primitive.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.5, p.50
exercise.description: Find 5 more Baudhāyana triples using the odd-square method (i.e., find odd perfect squares, identify n, and use (n−1)² + (2n−1) = n²).

items.section_title: Hypotenuse of an Isosceles Right Triangle
items.prompt: An isosceles right triangle has equal sides of length 7 units each. Find the exact length of its hypotenuse and determine between which two consecutive whole numbers the hypotenuse lies.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Using c² = 2a² with a = 7: c² = 2 × 49 = 98, so c = √98. Since 9² = 81 and 10² = 100, we have 9 < √98 < 10. The hypotenuse is √98, lying between 9 and 10.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply c² = 2a² to get c = √98, then bound by checking 9² = 81 < 98 < 100 = 10².

inclusivity.support: Draw the isosceles right triangle on squared paper and label the two equal sides 7; write c² = 2 × 7² before computing.
inclusivity.challenge: Narrow the bound further: determine whether √98 is closer to 9.8 or 9.9 by checking 9.8² and 9.9².

items.prompt: A right-angled triangle has one shorter side of length 9 cm and a hypotenuse of 41 cm. Using Baudhāyana's Theorem, find the length of the third side.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Baudhāyana's Theorem: a² + b² = c². With a = 9 and c = 41: b² = 41² − 9² = 1681 − 81 = 1600, so b = 40. The third side is 40 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Rearrange a² + b² = c² to b² = c² − a² = 1681 − 81 = 1600, giving b = 40.

inclusivity.support: Write the theorem as a² + b² = c², substitute the two known values, and isolate the unknown before computing.
inclusivity.challenge: Verify that (9, 40, 41) is a Baudhāyana triple and determine whether it is primitive or a scaled version of a smaller triple.

exercise.description: If a right-angled triangle has shorter sides of lengths 5 cm and 12 cm, what is the length of its hypotenuse? First draw and measure, then verify using Baudhāyana's Theorem.

items.section_title: Further Applications of the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem
items.prompt: A rhombus has diagonals of length 16 units and 30 units. Find the sidelength of the rhombus.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, forming four congruent right triangles with legs 8 and 15. By Baudhāyana's Theorem: s² = 8² + 15² = 64 + 225 = 289, so s = 17. The sidelength is 17 units.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Halve each diagonal to get legs 8 and 15, then apply a² + b² = c²: 64 + 225 = 289, giving side = 17.

inclusivity.support: Draw the rhombus and its two diagonals; mark where they cross and label the four half-lengths before applying the theorem.
inclusivity.challenge: Confirm that (8, 15, 17) is a primitive Baudhāyana triple, then state one other rectangle whose diagonal is also an integer.
